# Welcome {.unnumbered}

::: {.callout-important icon=false}
## Under construction

This book is being written. Chapters 1–10 are first drafts; every
other chapter is a placeholder that lists its planned topics, and the plan
itself will change. Nothing here is ready to teach from yet.
:::

Found a mistake, or a command that does not run for you? See
[Report an Issue](reporting.qmd), also linked from the bug icon at the top
of the left sidebar on every page.

*Computing for Bioinformatics* is the computing foundation for the series
*Bioinformatics: A Worked Approach*. It covers the Linux command line, HPC
and SLURM, R and Python for everyday analysis, file formats, reproducibility
(git, environments, containers), workflows (nf-core and Nextflow), and a
high-level tour of the algorithms behind common tools. The other books in
the series assume what is taught here.

## Who this book is for

- **MS and new PhD students with little computing background**, mostly from
  biology or animal science. Engineers and computer scientists are welcome,
  but will find the early chapters slow.
- **Beginner to intermediate.** You will mostly *use* existing tools,
  packages, and pipelines, not write them from scratch. Writing reusable
  code is covered, but it is optional and comes last.
- **You work, or will work, on a Linux HPC cluster** (e.g., SCINet
  Ceres/Atlas, ISU Nova), with a laptop for editing and small analyses.
  Readers without cluster access can still do the local examples and read
  the captured cluster output.

## What this book covers, and what it leaves out

The aim is **awareness, not depth**. Every core tool and idea a working
bioinformatician meets appears here, so that nothing in a later book is a
first encounter. Each topic gets the idea, why it matters, and a hands-on
use of the tool. Full algorithms (BLAST, Smith-Waterman, the FM-index,
assembly graphs) are left to the book that owns them, and linked forward.

This book also owns **file formats** for the series: FASTA, FASTQ, SAM/BAM,
BED, GFF, VCF, and friends are taught here, and other books link back.

**Why so much command line?** Most real bioinformatics runs on Linux
machines reached through a terminal: university clusters, and the cloud
servers that companies rent. So Part II teaches the Linux command line
and bash before any programming language, and the rest of the book
assumes them. @sec-shell-basics-why gives the reasons in full.

## How to read it

Every chapter carries one label:

- **Core** (24 chapters): work through it, with the exercises. The core
  chapters together are the first-pass path through the book.
- **Overview** (8 chapters): read for understanding; no required exercises.
  Explains why tools behave as they do.
- **Optional** (6 chapters): reference for later, when you need it.

Every command is marked with where it runs: your **laptop**, a cluster
**login node**, or a **compute node**.

The book uses one software setup throughout: a **pixi** environment for all
the tools, and **VS Code** as the editor, connected to a cluster by your site's
supported route. Both are set up in @sec-book-setup. A single running
dataset, a small yeast RNA-seq experiment from the nf-core/rnaseq test
data, is used from start to finish.
